title: Don't judge police over Taser incident without all the facts
article: I am sorry Trevor Grimolfson is dead. He may simply have needed help and now that help can never come.

I am especially sorry for his teenage children who, while not living with him at the time of his death, must now finish growing up without him, and for his parents and family who will have to find a way to live on without their "absolute sweetheart."

Grimolfson is the 38-year-old tattoo parlour owner who died along a dodgy strip of Edmonton's Stony Plain Road on Oct. 29 after coming to blows with someone in his own business, then tearing up a nearby pawnshop. He was Tasered by police when he resisted arrest.
I also feel sorry, though, for the police officers who twice discharged Tasers into the rampaging Grimolfson.
Just as Grimolfson didn't start off Wednesday looking to die, neither did the Edmonton Police Service members who subdued him start off hoping to be involved in his death.

Even if a coroner finds their actions did not contribute to his death and even if the new Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) -- an independent body established in January to investigate deaths or injuries resulting from police officers' actions -- ultimately exonerates their behaviour, the officers involved will always wonder whether there was something they could have done to make the outcome different, more benign.
In an understandable fit of grief and anger, Grimolfson's sister Mandie insisted her brother wasn't complicit in his own death. "Cops killed my brother."
But what else were police to do, confronted by a burly man who had allegedly assaulted two people, ransacked a pawnshop and was refusing to be arrested?
Would any of us have acted differently? None of us were there on the scene. We cannot know what officers saw, heard or felt.

We are in no position to second-guess their actions. That is for ASIRT, which is led by civilians and uses both civilian and police investigators to determine whether officers involved in serious or fatal incidents acted correctly.
Before we judge the officers involved too harshly, we have to know more about their actions and Grimolfson's.

One eyewitness to the tattoo artist's death, Michelle Furoy, manager of nearby Jasper Place Liquor, insists she is typically opposed to Taser use, but believes police were justified in discharging the weapons this time.

"The only other option was to shoot him," she told the Edmonton Journal. "That's how bad it was. . . . He was like a wild, rabid bear. He was just going crazy. I don't know what else they could have done."

Coming in the shadow of what now seems to be the obvious overreaction by RCMP at Vancouver International Airport last October, when they twice Tasered Polish immigrant Robert Dziekanski, who later died, many members of the public may want instantly to condemn the Edmonton officers involved in Grimolfson's death and those Calgary officers involved just days later in the death of Gordon Walker Bowe, 30, after they were called to a break and enter.
But it is far too early for such a judgment.

What is at play here are two conflicting impulses that will always be in conflict -- and should always be in conflict -- in a free society. Because the rule of law cedes to police a near-monopoly over the use of force, it is right to question each and every application of force by the police.
Yet at the same time, since most of us would not do what the police do even if given the chance under the law, we must guard against jumping to conclusions about their actions.

Few of us would confront a large, enraged man smashing apart a pawnshop or attempt to disband a gang loitering on a street corner, place ourselves in the middle of a family fight, attempt to arrest an armed robber or drug dealer, stare down a hostage taker or try to evict a disruptive drunk from a crowded bar. So we must be careful not to armchair quarterback those who do.
Our police are nearly always worthy of our support.
But I am beginning to wonder about the use of Tasers.

The victim of a robbery is far more likely to be injured or killed if his assailant is using a club or knife instead of a gun. According to Statistics Canada, victims robbed at gunpoint have a one-in-three chance of being injured. With a knife, the ratio is one in two, while with a club or a fist, the chances are four in five.

This is sometimes called the "facilitative effect." Victims confronted with a gun are far more likely to give their assailant what he wants, just as the gun-toting assailant, aware of the lethality of his tool, is more reluctant to attack.

Perhaps the Taser creates a similar facilitative effect: The alleged perpetrator is less likely to co-operate with Taser-wielding police, just as officers, assured in their minds that Tasers are less lethal, are more willing to fire them.

Since Dziekanski died last year, another seven Canadians have died after being Tasered by police. Perhaps it's time to consider whether their use is sometimes more dangerous than officers' use of guns.
